methodological_rigor.justification: The AIMS study uses a large, representative retrospective dataset of 50,000 women from two NHSBSP centers with prespecified 39-month follow-up, clear inclusion/exclusion criteria, and ISRCTN registration (no. 60839016). The paired-within-case design with reader-pair clustering, Obuchowski's extension of McNemar for clustered data, Holm-Bonferroni correction, prespecified 5% noninferiority margin, and an explicit simulation-based power calculation (200 positives/site for 80% power) are rigorous choices. Limitations acknowledged by authors include inability to blind the AI arm, identical noninferiority margins for sensitivity and specificity, exclusion of 8.7% of cases by AI criteria, and lack of multiplicity adjustment for exploratory subgroups. The study is retrospective with two centers only, and statistical noninferiority margin width may be seen as generous, preventing a 5.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective cohort-style diagnostic-accuracy study with an embedded prospective reader study for arbitration, mapping to Oxford 2b. The clinical relevance is high because it directly addresses whether AI can replace a second human reader within NHSBSP double-read-with-arbitration workflow, including a 46% reduction in screen reads and a quantified arbitration burden increase at each center. Findings inform near-term deployment decisions and upcoming prospective trials (e.g., EDITH) but are not yet practice-changing because the study is retrospective, single-vendor (Google v1.2), and confined to two London centers on predominantly Hologic equipment.

reporting_quality.justification: As a diagnostic-accuracy study with prespecified noninferiority endpoints, STARD is the most applicable standard, with TRIPOD-like elements for the AI model description. Reporting is thorough: clear flow of participants, exclusion accounting, predefined primary endpoint and margin, CIs and p-values throughout, subgroup caveats explicitly flagged as exploratory, and a reporting summary referenced. Source Data for Figs. 1-4 are cited and ethics/registration are stated, but there is no explicit repository DOI for patient-level data (OMI-DB access is restricted) and no AI model weights are shared, limiting reproducibility to a 3.

novelty_literature.justification: The paper fills a documented gap identified by the prior external validation pilot (ref. 4) calling for clinical validation of AI impact on arbitration. Unlike prior retrospective simulations of arbitration (refs. 2, 5-7) and the smaller 278-case reader study (ref. 8), this is a large-scale (45,602 women; 8,732 arbitrations; 22 readers) prospective reader arbitration using two NHSBSP-relevant arbitration protocols with long-term (39-month) follow-up, enabling earlier-detection and lesion-level analyses. The underlying AI tool and double-read paradigm are not new, so this is a novel combination and execution rather than first-in-class discovery.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well structured with a clear question, seven-aspect discussion framework, and informative tables (population, overall performance, workload, before/after arbitration). Figures 1-4 communicate study design, ROC comparisons, subgroup forest-style displays, and localization/FROC analyses effectively, with careful numeric labeling and CI reporting. Some tables (particularly Table 2 and Table 4) are dense and difficult to parse in text form, and terminology around "AI arm" versus "AI tool before arbitration" occasionally requires re-reading, preventing a 5.

key_strengths: Large, representative NHSBSP cohort (45,602 women) with 39-month follow-up enabling assessment of interval and next-round cancer detection
Prespecified 5% noninferiority margin, Holm-Bonferroni correction, and Obuchowski clustered-data inference on reader-pair clusters with explicit power simulation
Clinically realistic arbitration reader study with 22 accredited NHSBSP readers across two centers using both main NHSBSP arbitration protocols
Lesion-level JAFROC and ROI-overlap analysis illuminates why correct AI recalls are overruled (localization errors, superfluous ROIs, priors)
Quantified workload trade-off (46% fewer screen reads vs. 53% more arbitrations overall) supports deployment planning
key_concerns: Retrospective, two-center, single-vendor (Google v1.2) design on predominantly Hologic equipment limits generalizability, with a signal of worse AI performance on Siemens images
AI arm could not be blinded to readers, introducing potential bias acknowledged but not quantified
Same 5% noninferiority margin applied to specificity despite much larger negative sample, as authors themselves note
Subgroup analyses are underpowered (25/29 subgroups <300 positive cases) with no multiplicity adjustment, risking overinterpretation
Patient-level data and AI model weights are not openly available; reproducibility depends on OMI-DB and vendor access
After arbitration, the earlier-detection advantage for interval and next-round cancers largely disappears, tempering translational impact
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically solid, clinically important, adequately reported diagnostic-accuracy/reader study with a novel NHSBSP-specific arbitration contribution but retrospective two-center single-vendor design and a shrinking earlier-detection signal after arbitration. Tier 2 (e.g., Nature Communications, ESMO Open, Radiology AI) is the highest plausible acceptance venue with minor revisions.
